t01: Sentiment analysis decides whether text is positive, neutral, negative or mixed. Opinion mining is an extra option that pulls out the opinion (assessment) for each subject (target). Example: "The battery is great, but delivery was slow" → battery: positive, delivery: negative.
t02: Language detection is an Azure Language feature that recognizes which language a text is written in. You send text and get back a language code (for example nl, de, fr) with a confidence score between 0 and 1.
t03: Entity linking recognizes a name in the text and works out which real-world thing is meant. It returns a link to Wikipedia. Example: in "Mars launches a new bar", Mars is linked to the candy brand, not the planet.
t04: NER (named entity recognition) finds 'named things' in text and says what kind of thing each one is. Example: "Jan has worked at Microsoft in Amsterdam since March" → Jan = Person, March = DateTime, Microsoft = Organization, Amsterdam = Location. It only returns the category: no link and no custom types.
t05: PII = personally identifiable information: data that can identify a person (name, email, phone number, IBAN, social security number). PII detection finds it and also returns a version of the text with it masked (redactedText). A categories filter chooses which types; a redaction policy chooses what replaces them.
t06: Conversational PII is the same PII feature, but for conversations: you send the conversation as a list of messages with who is speaking (role) and in which order. It is meant for chats and transcribed phone calls.
t07: Text analytics for health is a medical version of Azure Language. It recognizes medical concepts (medication, dosage, diagnosis, symptom) and the relations between them, for example which dosage belongs to which medication.
t08: Extractive summarization builds a summary by picking the most important sentences word for word from the text. Each sentence gets a rank score (how important it is). No new sentences are added.
t09: Abstractive summarization writes a new, short summary in its own words, the way a person would. The sentences do not appear word for word in the source text.
t10: Conversation summarization is summarization built for conversations. You choose aspects: issue (what the problem was), resolution (how it was solved), chapter title (titles per part) or narrative (the story of the conversation).
t11: Custom text classification is a model you train yourself to put whole documents into categories. You provide examples with the correct label. Single-label = each document gets exactly one category.
t12: Custom text classification, multi-label: the same self-trained model, but one document can get several categories at once, for example 'billing' and 'technical issue'.
t13: Custom NER is NER with your own types of things. You mark in sample documents where, for example, the contract number and notice period are, train the model, and from then on it extracts those values from new documents.
t14: CLU (conversational language understanding) understands short commands or questions. It returns two things: the intent (what the user wants, for example MovePallet) and the entities (the values, for example pallet = 42, aisle = 7). You train it with example sentences called utterances.
t15: Custom question answering is a question-and-answer knowledge base. You load FAQ pages and documents, it turns them into question-answer pairs, and for a question it returns the best matching fixed answer. Follow-up prompts allow multi-turn conversations.
t16: An LLM (a large language model such as GPT-4.1) with structured outputs: you pass instructions and a JSON schema, and the model is guaranteed to return JSON in that shape. It can read, interpret and judge without being trained first.
t17: Document translation is an Azure Translator feature that translates whole files (Word, PDF, PowerPoint, Excel) and keeps the formatting. You put the files in a Blob Storage container (source), and the translated files appear in another container (target). It runs asynchronously: you start a job and collect the result later.
t18: A glossary is a file (for example CSV or TSV) listing terms and how they must be translated. In document translation it makes sure, for example, product names always stay the same.
t19: Dynamic dictionary is markup you put in the text of a text translation request itself, to force a word or name to a specific translation (or keep it untranslated).
t20: Custom Translator is a translation model you train yourself with parallel sentences: the same sentence in the source and target language. It learns the terminology and style of your domain. In your request you pass the category ID to use that model.
t21: Transliteration converts text to a different script without translating it. Example: Japanese characters to Latin letters (東京 → Tōkyō). The language and meaning stay the same.
t22: Text translation is the standard Azure Translator feature for plain text. You can request several target languages in one call with multiple 'to' parameters.
t23: Key phrase extraction pulls out the most important words or phrases from a text (for example 'battery life', 'fast delivery'). NER looks specifically for named things (people, places, organizations) and says which type each one is.
t24: Three self-trained Azure Language models with different outputs: classification labels the whole document, custom NER extracts specific pieces of text, and CLU returns both the intent and the values for short commands.
t25: Azure Language is a set of ready-made language features (fixed output, cheap per document). An LLM is a general language model that you can instruct to do almost anything, but it is more expensive and less predictable.
t26: A container is a packaged version of an Azure service that you run on your own server with Docker. The data stays local. Connected: the container only reports usage (for billing) to Azure. When starting it you must pass Eula=accept, Billing (the endpoint of your Azure resource) and ApiKey.
s01: Speech to text (STT) turns spoken language into text. Real time means: while someone is speaking, through the Speech SDK (the Azure Speech programming library), for example from a microphone.
s02: recognize_once_async() listens until the first pause and returns one sentence. start_continuous_recognition() keeps listening and passes every recognized sentence to your code through events, until you stop it.
s03: Batch transcription processes large numbers of audio files asynchronously: you point it at a Blob Storage container, the service works through everything, and you collect the results later. Diarization is the option that separates the speakers.
s04: Fast transcription is an API that transcribes one audio file in a single request and returns the result immediately (synchronous). Faster than batch for individual files.
s05: Diarization recognizes who speaks when. The transcript then gets labels such as Speaker 1 and Speaker 2.
s06: A phrase list is a list of words or phrases you pass to the recognizer so it recognizes those words better. No training, immediate effect.
s07: Custom speech is a speech recognition model you train further with your own data: texts with jargon, or recordings with the correct transcript. You measure quality with WER (word error rate: the percentage of words recognized wrongly) and use it through your own endpoint (endpoint_id).
s08: SSML (Speech Synthesis Markup Language) is a kind of HTML for speech. Tags control how text is spoken: say-as (for example as digits or a date), break (a pause), prosody (speed, pitch, volume).
s09: Speaking styles make a neural voice speak with a certain emotion or tone, such as cheerful or empathetic. You set this in SSML with the mstts:express-as element.
s10: Custom neural voice is your own unique computer voice, built from recordings of a voice actor. It requires Limited Access (an application to Microsoft) and the speaker's consent.
s11: Speech translation recognizes spoken language and translates it in one step into one or more other languages, as text and optionally as speech. In code: a TranslationRecognizer with add_target_language for each target language.
s12: The Voice Live API is a real-time connection (WebSocket) for spoken conversations with AI. It includes speech recognition, the language model and speech output, plus turn detection (knowing when the user has finished) and noise suppression. That keeps latency low and lets the user interrupt.
s13: Language identification is an Azure Speech feature that recognizes which language is being spoken, from a list of candidate languages you provide.
s14: Content Understanding is a Foundry service that turns content (documents, images, audio, video) into structured fields. prebuilt-callCenter is a ready-made analyzer for calls: topics, sentiment and a summary.
s15: Custom speech improves how the computer understands speech (speech → text). Custom neural voice gives the computer its own voice (text → speech). Opposite directions.
s16: A phrase list is a quick fix for a few words. Custom speech is a trained model for structural problems such as jargon, accents or background noise.
s17: Three ways to transcribe speech: real time (live, while speaking), fast (one file, immediate answer) and batch (many files at once, ready later).
